FAST FOOD TO MED SCHOOL

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Popular Little Gujarat restauranteers caught selling more than their famous vegetarian bunny chows – med school spots go for up to R500 000.

Unique Selling Point:
UNBELIEVABLE CORRUPTION

AUDIO RECORDINGS OF UNDERCOVER NEGOTIATIONS FOR A SPOT IN MED SCHOOL

NOT COVERED WELL NATIONALLY - ONLY RECEIVED COVERAGE IN DURBAN - HUGE NATIONAL APPEAL AND WE MAKE VIEWERS HAPPY WITH A DURBAN STORY.

Summary:
Indian Restaurant Owners - the Bhatts - sell a lot more than just good food - you can buy a prized spot in UKZN's medical school fora fee.

Their syndicate have been exposed and the worms seem to be coming out of the woodwork.

We bring you this almost unbelievable story of corruption all from a little curry spot in Durban.

Further information:
The owners of popular Little Gujarat restaurants were caught selling more than their famous vegetarian bunny chows this week.
Police suspect Varsha, 44, and Hiteshkumar Bhatt, 46, and a former Chatsworth school teacher, Preshni Hiramun, 54, are the masterminds who sold medicine and other health science places at the University of KwaZulu-Natal for up to R500 000.
On Friday, an elite team from the Hawks Organised Crime Unit and the National Intervention Unit (NIU) raided the homes and businesses of three people. The probe was led by investigating officer Mandla Mkhwanazi and Constable Nomfanelo Mabaso.
The trio was charged with fraud and contravention of the Prevention and Combating of Corrupt Activities Act.
The three are accused of working as agents in cahoots with a syndicate at UKZN to fraudulently enrol students in the health science faculty and school of medicine.
There is also evidence to suggest they have links to a syndicate at the Sefako Makgatho Health Sciences University, once known as the Medical University of South Africa.
Friday’s raids were conducted at the couple’s upmarket homes in La Lucia and uMhlanga as well as their businesses.
Little Gujarat, in the Durban CBD, came to a standstill as customers watched as the police swooped, seizing assets belonging to the Bhatts, including two Mercedes-Benz vehicles, laptops, hard-drives and flash drives.
At Hiramun’s home in Somerset Park, uMhlanga, laptops were found hidden in a washing machine.
Evidence, such as documents pertaining to the syndicate, was also seized.
It is alleged the Bhatts and Hiramun acted as agents. They chatted to interested parents, negotiated bribes and liaised with university staff who helped get the parents’ children enrolled.
This was done even though the students involved did not meet the minimum requirements for the courses.
The three suspects allegedly charged R250 000 for admission to the health sciences faculty. This included pharmacy, optometry and audiology. They charged R500 000 for a place in medicine.
It is further claimed the trio were involved in the sale of examination question and answer papers for an additional R30 000.
The arrests followed a sting operation by the Hawks during this year’s admission period from February to March, where students were admitted into the university for a bribe.
The suspects were held over the weekend at the Westville SAPS and were expected to appear in court tomorrow.
KZN Hawks spokesperson Captain Simphiwe Mhlongo confirmed the arrests and said the probe was at a sensitive stage. Mhlongo said more arrests were imminent.
An investigation into their affairs was prompted in January when UKZN vice-chancellor Professor Albert van Jaarsveld handed information against the syndicate to the Hawks.
Van Jaarsveld welcomed the arrests. He said UKZN would not tolerate fraud within the institution and would apply appropriate prevention and detection controls.
“All fraud will be investigated and followed up by the application of all remedies available to the full extent of the law,” he said.
In June, the Sunday Tribune exposed the work of an alleged syndicate. During the course of the probe, this newspaper interacted with the arrested suspects and recorded a series of conversations in which negotiations took place to admit a student to UKZN to study pharmacy.
The university subsequently asked KPMG to conduct a forensic audit. Police have now asked those who may be involved in the syndicate, including students fraudulently admitted, to come forward before they are caught. UKZN has set up a toll-free fraud hotline number, 0800 203 285.
Who are the Bhatts?
Hitesh and Varsha Bhatt are well known for their bunny chows and for the Little Gujarat restaurant, which CNN declared last year one of the world’s best for street food.
The couple came to South Africa in 1990 from Gujarat, India, after Hitesh decided to follow his father and open a business here.
His father opened the first Little Gujarat store in Bertha Mkhize (Victoria) Street in 1989 and it became a hit.
Today the couple owns a string of businesses, including restaurants, an Eastern wear boutique in the CBD and an investment company.
As the couple’s restaurant was raided on Friday, people from neighbouring businesses said the Bhatts were respected, long-standing tenants at Dr Goonam (Prince Edward) Street.
WHAT WE HAVE
• Audio recordings of an undercover sting negotiating a spot at medical school for a fee.
• Footage of the arrests
• Two med students that didn’t get in despite their good marks
• A family that entered into negotiations but decided not to go through with it – HIDDEN IDENTITY

Press Release:


From Bunny Chows to Medical School
2
How are the owners of a popular fast food restaurant in Durban linked to the sale of more than just their famous vegetarian bunny chows? It seems you could pick up a
take-away and for another R500 000 you could also buy your child a coveted spot at a prized medical school. Carte Blanche investigates how fraudsters linked to a local
university pulled off a clever scheme to not only make fast food, but also a quick buck.
Producer: Nicky Troll
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: While many children dream of becoming medical doctors, very few will make the leap from playing pretend to real life.

LINK: Even straight A’s won’t guarantee you a spot in medical school – race and the kind of school you went to all play role – at the University of KwaZulu Natal in just this year there were almost 7000 applicants for 250 spots – calling for very inventive solutions.

UPSOUND AUDIO RECORDING FEBRUARY 2017 – VOICE OF PRESHNI HIRAMUN:
PRESHNI: // For medicine it’s about R550k and pharmacy it’s R250k // If you want medicine – then we can do something in October this year.

VO: A Durban syndicate stands accused of selling placements at UKZN’s medical school.

Central to the scandal is: Little Gujarat restaurant owners Varsha & Hitesh Bhatt, and a former school teacher Preshni Hiramun.

NABEELAH: They were allegedly agents in this syndicate, doing the negotiations to get the students in, meeting with parents, exchaning the moneys.

LINK: It’s an unlikely combination; you’d expect fragrant curries to come out of a kitchen like this but not a back door entry into medical school.

VO: Reporter Nabeelah Shaikh has been following this story for 18 months.

NABEELAH: // the allegation is that they have been working with a cabal of staff within the institution// high ranking academics and admin staff who were working to admit these students into the institute despite them not meeting the criteria.

INSIDER: what I can tell you – this is not new… // The corruption is at the highest level!

VO: A UKZN Medical School Faculty board member who asked not be identified, spoke to us about what he calls the rot within the institution.

INSIDER: // If there are regulations there – you need to follow them // why would you want to bend the rules // there is only one reason is money.

VO: The lid on the alleged corruption was lifted by this email from a whistleblower, employed at the UKZN Medical School admin in 2016.

“In 2015 and 2016 many Indian children with low averages are being registered for MBCHB. I questioned this with my superiors but was shut down because they told me that I must do my job and not worry about a matter of this nature.”

NABEELAH: The whistleblower came forward with a list of names of students who she thought could have been potentially illegally enrolled because they did not meet the criteria and she also made the allegation that they were passing themselves off as coloured to cheat the system and get in // and then doing further investigations into the allegations, we realised that there was something with the intake in that particular year.

VO: The UKZN’s Medical School has a strict quota policy aimed at levelling the playing field so that all race groups get an equal opportunity – but it also adds to the competition for the limited number of spaces available.

IRSHAAD: // in South Africa, we have a lack of medical school seats, // so the ones that do get accepted // are lucky – the rest have to find alternatives if medicine is really a dream //.

VO: Dr Irshaad Saley was not one of the lucky ones in 2007. His five distinctions didn’t get him in to study medicine at UKZN.

IRSHAAD: I just lost hope, and I didn’t want to do it any more // until my father convinced us to go to China.
DEVI: Did you hear rumours before that you could buy a place?
IRSHAAD: Yes, we did, prior to going to China we actually did hear // we said no, that’s not the right thing to do, so we didn’t even pursue that way.

VO: But while thousands of students are finding legitimate ways to study medicine, an elite group are buying their way in.

This recording is of former school teacher Preshni Hiramun speaking to a prospective parent, even she bemoans the quota system.

PRESHNI: // it hurts us, but either way that’s what people do to us, but that’s the way life is…

VO: But where there is a will, there is often an alternative way…

PRESHNI: // but these people generally know how to work their books

LINK: A leaked KPMG report found that admissions were taking place contrary to the medical school’s policy.

NABEELAH: // that in itself tells you there was a flaw in the system and that there were people on the inside who were intentionally regretting students simply so that they could make more spaces for these other students that were willing to pay a bribe.

VO: Agent Preshni explained that when students who meet the admissions criteria don’t take up the medical school placement, a vacant spot is created.

PRESHNI: They have a reserve list that they must choose from, but they don’t take, that’s when they slot like your daughter, when they get the cancellations.

VO: Ameera Suleman was one of the thousands of students that received a letter of regret from UKZN in 2016 - despite having 7 A’s and an aggregate in the 90’s.

AMEERA: Now that we hear about this bribe – it can kind of leads to the question if someone bought the place that you could have had

VO: She has opted to pursue a career in pharmacy and is currently in her second year of studies.

DEVI: IS it life changing when something like that happens?
AMeERA: it changes the course of your life – I am on a totally different course because of this probably.

VO: Department of Higher Education and Training has an oversight role for universities.

DIANE: This is not just about one institution – this is about the credibility of the system.

VO: Dr Diane Parker is the Deputy Director General for Universities – she says there will be consequences.

DIANE: Individuals whoever they are, at whatever level they are within the institution that allowed this to happen need to be brought to book, the need to be disciplined – we need to ensure that we’ve got integrity within our system //

VO: A system that agent Preshni is confident they can manipulate.

PRESHNI: With the 81% I can get you medicine – anything above 80% I can get you in, but below that, I can’t touch you

NABEELAH: But even still 80% would not have been good enough for an Indian student considering that they needed 90.83% to get in, in 2017.

INSIDER: there are processes and regulations that need to be followed and these were not followed!

VO: UKZN’s Vice Chancellor Dr Albert van Jaarsveld, declined to comment saying they are working closely with law enforcement agencies and “divulging further information at this stage will be prejudicial to the outcome of the investigation.”

A HAWKS sting operation linking the three agents – lead to Varsha & Hitesh Bhatt, and Preshni Hiramun’s arrest in May - for corruption relating to the sale medical school placements. They are currently out on bail of R40 000 each.

We paid Little Gujarat a visit… Varsha Bhatt was behind the counter while out on bail.

DEVI: Is it true that you were selling medical degrees?
VARSHA: No, look at how my business – I don’t know how to do proper all the things
DEVI: Why are they blaming you guys?
VARSHA: That’s why I say talk to my lawyer.
DEVI: And Preshni Hiramun – you don’t work with her?
VARSHA: No…no,
DEVI: Do you know her?
VARSHA: uh, no… you can talk to my lawyer.

VO: Their lawyer declined to comment.

UPSOUND ROY SINGH:

VO: When we spoke to Preshni, she did not deny that it was her in the audio recordings.

PRESHNI A lot of things have been said, a lot of lies have been said and at the end of the day – Varsha and I are both innocent
DEVI: I asked Varsha – do you know Preshni Hiramun – and she said no, //
PRESHNI: I suppose everyone is just scared they don’t know who they can trust.
DEVI: Ja, scared, but don’t lie.

VO: While the desire to study medicine outweighs universities capacity to teach medicine - unscrupulous people will take the gap.

NABEELAH: there are not enough medical universities to study because people are willing o go to the extent to go and pay half a million rand to secure a place for their child to just get an education.

DEVI: Why not take 50 students?
DIANE: Because of the strict situation around the accreditation of medical programmes, that is very expensive and so you know, just saying take 50 more is not that easy – you have find the financing for it – however working with the department of health we have been pushing the expansion of medical education and we are working towards the development of new medical schools.

VO: But until then there will be a demand and someone willing to supply.

PRESHNI All I want to say to you is, simple, you get the middleman, you get the buyer and the receiver.
DEVI: Then who was in the middle?
PRESHNI: They calling us the middle.
DEVI: ja, that’s what they saying.
PRESHNI: It’s simple…How do you arrest one without the others?

VO: Preshni can rest assured – the police say more arrests will follow. While those pulling the strings will face criminal charges, it’s unclear as to how the beneficiaries will be impacted.

DIANE: Difficult to take degree away…. // Whether or not there is criminal action or disciplinary action against them by the institution or by the law enforcement agencies – they will be affected in terms of if that becomes public.

VO: Chinese Medical School graduate, Dr. Saley doesn’t regret going overseas - because it seems those that bent the rules will pay in the long run.

IRSHAAD: We didn’t do anything illegal, we did it the hard way, but we did it the right way, we can sleep easy now, knowing nobody is going to go come take our degree away, nobody is going to come knock on our door


PROMOS

PROMO 1
PRESHNI: For medicine it’s about R550k and pharmacy it’s R250k

VO: A spot to study medicine at UKZN for fee exposed.


PROMO 2
VO: From selling vegetarian bunny chows, to selling a prized spot at UKZN's medical school – a durban syndicate is alleged to have been coining it.

NABEELAH: // the allegation is that they have been working with a cabal of staff within the institution
PROMO 3
VO: Even with straight A’s it’s tough getting into medical school, but if you can you cough up half a million rand you could buy yourself a spot.

PRESHNI: For medicine it’s about R550k and pharmacy it’s R250k

PRESHNI: They have a reserve list that they must choose from, but they don’t take, that’s when they slot like your daughter, when they get the cancellations. VO: Ameera Suleman was one of the thousands of students that received a letter of regret from UKZN in 2016 - despite having 7 A’s and an aggregate in the 90’s. AMEERA: Now that we hear about this bribe – it can kind of leads to the question if someone bought the place that you could have had VO: She has opted to pursue a career in pharmacy and is currently in her second year of studies. DEVI: IS it life changing when something like that happens? AMeERA: it changes the course of your life – I am on a totally different course because of this probably. VARSHA: No, look at how my business – I don’t know how to do proper all the things DEVI: Why are they blaming you guys? VARSHA: That’s why I say talk to my lawyer. UPSOUND ROY SINGH: VO: When we spoke to Preshni, she did not deny that it was her in the audio recordings. PRESHNI A lot of things have been said, a lot of lies have been said and at the end of the day – Varsha and I are both innocent DEVI: I asked Varsha – do you know Preshni Hiramun – and she said no, // PRESHNI: I suppose everyone is just scared they don’t know who they can trust. DEVI: Ja, scared, but don’t lie. VO: While the desire to study medicine outweighs universities capacity to teach medicine - unscrupulous people will take the gap. metadata.Summary: Indian Restaurant Owners - the Bhatts - sell a lot more than just good food - you can buy a prized spot in UKZN's medical school fora fee. Their syndicate have been exposed and the worms seem to be coming out of the woodwork. We bring you this almost unbelievable story of corruption all from a little curry spot in Durban.
metadata.Further information: The owners of popular Little Gujarat restaurants were caught selling more than their famous vegetarian bunny chows this week. Police suspect Varsha, 44, and Hiteshkumar Bhatt, 46, and a former Chatsworth school teacher, Preshni Hiramun, 54, are the masterminds who sold medicine and other health science places at the University of KwaZulu-Natal for up to R500 000. On Friday, an elite team from the Hawks Organised Crime Unit and the National Intervention Unit (NIU) raided the homes and businesses of three people. The probe was led by investigating officer Mandla Mkhwanazi and Constable Nomfanelo Mabaso. The trio was charged with fraud and contravention of the Prevention and Combating of Corrupt Activities Act. The three are accused of working as agents in cahoots with a syndicate at UKZN to fraudulently enrol students in the health science faculty and school of medicine. There is also evidence to suggest they have links to a syndicate at the Sefako Makgatho Health Sciences University, once known as the Medical University of South Africa. Friday’s raids were conducted at the couple’s upmarket homes in La Lucia and uMhlanga as well as their businesses. Little Gujarat, in the Durban CBD, came to a standstill as customers watched as the police swooped, seizing assets belonging to the Bhatts, including two Mercedes-Benz vehicles, laptops, hard-drives and flash drives. At Hiramun’s home in Somerset Park, uMhlanga, laptops were found hidden in a washing machine. Evidence, such as documents pertaining to the syndicate, was also seized. It is alleged the Bhatts and Hiramun acted as agents. They chatted to interested parents, negotiated bribes and liaised with university staff who helped get the parents’ children enrolled. This was done even though the students involved did not meet the minimum requirements for the courses. The three suspects allegedly charged R250 000 for admission to the health sciences faculty. This included pharmacy, optometry and audiology. They charged R500 000 for a place in medicine. It is further claimed the trio were involved in the sale of examination question and answer papers for an additional R30 000. The arrests followed a sting operation by the Hawks during this year’s admission period from February to March, where students were admitted into the university for a bribe. The suspects were held over the weekend at the Westville SAPS and were expected to appear in court tomorrow. KZN Hawks spokesperson Captain Simphiwe Mhlongo confirmed the arrests and said the probe was at a sensitive stage. Mhlongo said more arrests were imminent. An investigation into their affairs was prompted in January when UKZN vice-chancellor Professor Albert van Jaarsveld handed information against the syndicate to the Hawks. Van Jaarsveld welcomed the arrests. He said UKZN would not tolerate fraud within the institution and would apply appropriate prevention and detection controls. “All fraud will be investigated and followed up by the application of all remedies available to the full extent of the law,” he said. In June, the Sunday Tribune exposed the work of an alleged syndicate. During the course of the probe, this newspaper interacted with the arrested suspects and recorded a series of conversations in which negotiations took place to admit a student to UKZN to study pharmacy. The university subsequently asked KPMG to conduct a forensic audit. Police have now asked those who may be involved in the syndicate, including students fraudulently admitted, to come forward before they are caught. UKZN has set up a toll-free fraud hotline number, 0800 203 285. Who are the Bhatts? Hitesh and Varsha Bhatt are well known for their bunny chows and for the Little Gujarat restaurant, which CNN declared last year one of the world’s best for street food. The couple came to South Africa in 1990 from Gujarat, India, after Hitesh decided to follow his father and open a business here. His father opened the first Little Gujarat store in Bertha Mkhize (Victoria) Street in 1989 and it became a hit. Today the couple owns a string of businesses, including restaurants, an Eastern wear boutique in the CBD and an investment company. As the couple’s restaurant was raided on Friday, people from neighbouring businesses said the Bhatts were respected, long-standing tenants at Dr Goonam (Prince Edward) Street. WHAT WE HAVE • Audio recordings of an undercover sting negotiating a spot at medical school for a fee. • Footage of the arrests • Two med students that didn’t get in despite their good marks • A family that entered into negotiations but decided not to go through with it – HIDDEN IDENTITY WILL ADD SPECIFIC DETAILS OF CASE STUDIES AS SOON AS I HAVE THEM
